title: Enterprise reserved capacity intake rubric: QoS classes, GPU selection, and scaling scenarios
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Purpose: Create a pragmatic intake rubric and prioritization guide for enterprise reserved capacity requests that balances SLA targets, guaranteed throughput, GPU class selection, burst behaviour, and upgrade/fallback policies. Background: We receive high-variance enterprise requests requesting different mixes of latency, sustained throughput, and cost constraints. Current ad-hoc intake leads to inconsistent sizing, surprised customers, and back-and-forth on GPU selection and burst allowances. Goal: Ship a repeatable rubric that Product, Sales Engineering, and Solutions can use to 1) map customer requirements to QoS tiers, 2) recommend GPU family and quantization profile, 3) define reserved baseline vs burst policy, and 4) encode escalation/rollout guidance for Dedicated onboarding.
scope: Deliver one intake questionnaire template, a decision matrix (QoS x throughput x GPU class), recommended defaults for burst/preemption, and a short runbook for SalesEng to use during contract negotiation. This ticket does NOT include console UI changes; those will be a follow-up (PM-XXXXX).
acceptance_criteria: A1: Intake questionnaire covers SLA latency (p50/p95), steady-state throughput (tokens/s), burst traffic pattern (burst QPS and duration), model family plus acceptable quantization, geographic region, and data residency requirements.

A2: Decision matrix maps customer requirements to one of three QoS tiers (Gold / Silver / Bronze) with explicit guidance on expected latency SLOs, recommended GPU families (A100/H100/L40x), and minimum reserved throughput in GPU slots and tokens/s.
A3: Burst policy template defines burst allowance (x% of baseline), max burst duration, and degradation strategy (graceful fallback to smaller model or queue), acceptable to Support and SRE.
A4: Cost/contract note explains trade-offs and includes an expected monthly cost delta estimate based on GPU family and reservation size.
A5: SalesEng / Solutions runbook validated in a dry-run with two customer scenarios and feedback captured.
A6: Published Confluence doc and a short internal 1-pager shared with GTM and Solutions teams.
A7: Dependencies called out (billing, infra quotas) and at least one dependency owner assigned.
A8: Security and compliance checklist included for Private/VPC customers and marked if HSM/KMS required.
A9: Stakeholders sign off: PM, two SalesEngineers, Infra lead, and SRE on rollback and fallback behaviour.
A10: Example sizing calculation included for a representative customer using a 30-day traffic trace (synthetic) demonstrating SLO math.
decisions: D1: QoS tiers will be Gold (low-latency p95 target <= 150ms for short sequences), Silver (p95 <= 350ms), Bronze (best-effort with throughput guarantees).
D2: GPU family defaults: H100 for Gold with vectorized kernels, A100 for Silver, L40x or T4-equivalent for Bronze (if quantization allowed).
D3: Minimum reservation expressed as a combination of: concurrent GPU slots + guaranteed tokens/s budget, rather than raw GPU count alone.
D4: Burst allowance default = 2x baseline for up to 10 minutes, with automatic fallback to a lower-cost model variant if sustained beyond burst window.
D5: Preemption policy: Reserved capacity will be non-preemptible for Gold; Silver may be preemptible outside business hours where customer agrees.
D6: Automation: Recommend a console flag for 'Enterprise QoS tier' to later tie to autoscaling and billing (follow-up ticket).
tradeoffs: T1: Selecting H100 by default for Gold increases committed cost but reduces variability and simplifies kernel choices — trade-off between predictability and cost.
T2: Expressing reservations as tokens/s + slots improves characterization but requires billing and telemetry changes.
T3: Aggressive burst allowances can improve customer experience at the cost of higher tail capacity requirements; we propose a conservative default with opt-in higher burst SLAs.
T4: Allowing preemptible Silver capacity can save cost but increases complexity in client-side retry/fallback logic.
T5: Keeping the first pass as a runbook + manual template vs building a UI reduces initial engineering effort but increases risk of human error in sales negotiations.
